---
title: "Out-of-Distribution (OOD)"
description: "An input is out-of-distribution when it differs in relevant ways from the data distribution a model was trained or validated on."
term: "Out-of-Distribution (OOD)"
letter: "O"
category: "Model Evaluation"
difficulty: "Advanced"
---

## Simple explanation

An out-of-distribution (OOD) input comes from a setting that differs from
what a model learned from. A model trained on daytime road images, for
example, may encounter night scenes or a new camera type.

## Technical explanation

Let training examples be drawn from a distribution $P_{\text{train}}$ and
deployment inputs from $P_{\text{deploy}}$. An input is considered OOD
when its relevant characteristics are not adequately represented by the
training distribution. This can involve covariate, label, or concept shift,
and the exact definition depends on the task.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

OOD inputs can cause unreliable predictions, especially when models remain
confident outside their training experience. Engineers use representative
testing, monitoring, uncertainty estimates, and escalation policies to
reduce risk; no single detector identifies every kind of distribution
change.

## How it works

OOD detection methods may use confidence or energy scores, distances in a
representation space, density estimates, or auxiliary data. A detector
compares a score with a threshold, but the threshold and method should be
evaluated against realistic in-distribution and OOD examples.

## Practical example

A medical-image model developed at one hospital may be tested on images
from a different scanner and patient population. A performance drop or
unusual input statistics can signal a distribution shift and trigger
additional review rather than automatic reliance on predictions.

## Common misconceptions

- OOD is relative to the training and deployment context, not an absolute property of an input.
- Distribution shift does not always mean every prediction is wrong, and in-distribution inputs can still be misclassified.
- High model confidence does not prove that an input is in-distribution.
